title: Data interception and theft
starter: You are working on a train and open your email over the free Wi-Fi. List everything that could go wrong, and what would prevent each one.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Data interception and theft
facts: Data is captured as it travels across a network, without the sender or receiver knowing.
Attackers can also steal data at rest: from a stolen laptop, USB stick or printout.
The aim is usually personal details, passwords or company secrets.
stations.challenge: Write a definition of data interception and theft.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Data is captured as it travels across a network, without the sender or receiver knowing.
Also credit: Attackers can also steal data at rest: from a stolen laptop, USB stick or printout.

questions.a: Capturing data as it travels across a network

questions.q: Which is an example of data theft rather than interception?
questions.a: A laptop full of customer records is stolen from a car

stations.name: Packet sniffing
facts: Packet sniffer software captures the packets travelling on a network.
Network managers use it legitimately to find faults; attackers use the same tools to steal data.
Unsecured or public Wi-Fi makes sniffing much easier.
stations.challenge: Name a piece of software or hardware used for packet sniffing.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Packet sniffer software captures the packets travelling on a network.
Also credit: Network managers use it legitimately to find faults; attackers use the same tools to steal data.

questions.q: What does packet sniffer software do?
questions.a: Captures and examines the packets travelling across a network

questions.q: Why is free public Wi-Fi risky?
questions.a: Traffic may be unencrypted, and anyone nearby could capture it

stations.name: Man in the middle
facts: The attacker sits between you and the service, passing messages on.
Both sides think they're talking directly to each other.
A fake Wi-Fi hotspot, such as 'Free Airport WiFi', is a common trick.
stations.challenge: Why is a fake hotspot so effective?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The attacker sits between you and the service, passing messages on.
Also credit: Both sides think they're talking directly to each other.

questions.q: In a man-in-the-middle attack, what does the attacker do?
questions.a: Sits between the two parties, reading and passing on the messages

questions.q: Which warning sign might suggest a fake hotspot?
questions.a: An open network with a convincing name and no password

stations.name: What attackers gain
facts: Usernames and passwords typed into unencrypted sites.
Bank details, private messages and company documents.
Enough personal information to commit identity fraud.
stations.challenge: What could someone do with an intercepted school login?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Usernames and passwords typed into unencrypted sites.
Also credit: Bank details, private messages and company documents.

questions.q: Why is intercepted data valuable to criminals?
questions.a: It can be used for fraud, or sold to others

questions.q: Which everyday habit most increases the risk of data theft?
questions.a: Writing passwords down and leaving them by the computer

stations.name: Encryption is the answer
facts: Encryption scrambles data so intercepted packets are useless without the key.
HTTPS encrypts traffic between a browser and a website; WPA2 encrypts Wi-Fi.
A VPN encrypts everything between your device and a trusted server.
stations.challenge: Why does encryption not stop interception, but still protect you?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Encryption scrambles data so intercepted packets are useless without the key.
Also credit: HTTPS encrypts traffic between a browser and a website; WPA2 encrypts Wi-Fi.

questions.q: How does encryption protect data in transit?
questions.a: Intercepted data can't be understood without the key
Encrypts all your traffic between your device and a trusted server

stations.name: Other protections
facts: Don't send sensitive data over open Wi-Fi; use mobile data or a VPN.
Log off, lock screens and shred printouts.
Physical security: locked server rooms and cabinets.
Access levels mean a stolen login only reaches part of the data.
stations.challenge: List five things a company could do to reduce data interception and theft.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Don't send sensitive data over open Wi-Fi; use mobile data or a VPN.
Also credit: Log off, lock screens and shred printouts.

questions.q: Which of these reduce the risk of data interception and theft? Select all that apply.
questions.a: Using HTTPS and WPA2 encryption; Using a VPN on public Wi-Fi; Locking screens and logging off; Shredding printouts with personal data

final.name: Final challenge: safe or risky?

questions.q: Is each habit safe or risky?
questions.a: Banking on open café Wi-Fi with no VPN = Risky; Checking the padlock and HTTPS before logging in = Safe; Leaving a laptop unlocked at a desk = Risky; Shredding printouts containing customer details = Safe; Writing the Wi-Fi password on the office whiteboard = Risky; Using a VPN when working away from the office = Safe; Emailing a spreadsheet of personal data unencrypted = Risky; Keeping the server room locked = Safe

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe how data can be intercepted as it travels across a network.
points: Data is captured as it travels across a network, without the sender or receiver knowing.
Packet sniffer software captures the packets travelling on a network.
Network managers use it legitimately to find faults; attackers use the same tools to steal data.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Explain why encryption makes intercepted data useless to an attacker.
points: Encryption scrambles data so intercepted packets are useless without the key.
Unsecured or public Wi-Fi makes sniffing much easier.
The attacker sits between you and the service, passing messages on.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

points: Data is captured as it travels across a network, without the sender or receiver knowing.

The aim is usually personal details, passwords or company secrets.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
